::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### A note on platforms {#a-note-on-platforms}

This tutorial assumes a **Linux-like terminal** — bash or zsh on macOS, Linux,
GitHub Codespaces, or similar (see [How to use this
article](#choose-your-environment)). That is where most AI tooling, containers,
and CI pipelines expect you to work.

On **Windows**, things can look a little different: keyboard shortcuts, path
separators (`\` vs `/`), and some command names may not match. **WSL**
(Windows Subsystem for Linux) or **Git Bash** are good ways to follow along with
minimal friction. If you are using PowerShell or Command Prompt, treat this
guide as conceptually useful, but expect differences in detail.
:::

## Introduction

If you build AI products, sooner or later you end up stitching together a
small orchestra of tools:

- local scripts
- API calls
- logs
- config files
- containers
- CI pipelines

The shell is often the quickest way to make these components cooperate.
This tutorial covers **just enough** shell to survive day-to-day AI engineering —
navigation, safety habits, glue pipelines, and hands-on challenges — without
pretending you need to become a terminal wizard.

### Intended Audience

Engineers who are comfortable writing code but have little (or no) shell
experience. If you are already fluent in shell, skip ahead to
[process control and service debugging](#processes-ports-and-signals).

### What You'll Need

- [ ] A **terminal** — the window where you type shell commands (also called a
  shell or command line)
- [ ] Basic familiarity with files and folders
- [ ] Curiosity and willingness to try small experiments

## How To Use This Article {#choose-your-environment}

Pick how you want to follow along. The **browser sandbox** is the default for
interactive challenges; switch to a **local terminal** or **GitHub Codespaces**
when an exercise needs keyboard shortcuts, process control, or tools the sandbox
does not provide.

### Local terminal {#local-terminal}

```{=html}
<a id="local-terminal"></a>
```

Your machine's own shell — Terminal.app or iTerm on macOS, the default terminal
on Linux, **WSL** or **Git Bash** on Windows, or similar.

**Getting started**

- Open your terminal application and follow the **Try It** steps in each section.
- Challenge **Check my work** buttons target the browser sandbox only — here you
  self-check against the expected output described in each exercise.

**What you get**

- Real process IDs, signals, ports, and filesystem behaviour.

**Platform notes**

- This tutorial assumes a **Linux-like** shell (bash or zsh). See [A note on
  platforms](#a-note-on-platforms) for Windows differences.
- Your config files (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc`) and command history behave as on
  any normal system.

**Best for**

- Tab completion, modifier-key practice, Ctrl+R, process debugging (section 7),

### A few words we reuse constantly {#core-vocabulary}

- **Command** — a program name you type at the prompt (e.g. `ls`, `grep`)
- **Flag** — an option after a command, usually starting with `-` (e.g. `ls -la`)
- **Pipeline** — commands chained with `|`, where each command's output feeds the
  next (covered properly in [section 2](#data-flow-pipes-and-redirection))
- **Prompt** — the line where you type, ending in `$` (or `%` on some shells)

See the full [Glossary](#glossary) at the end of this article for every command
and term with links back to where it is introduced.

## Hints and Tips

A handful of habits that pay off immediately. These are worth learning early,
before the command vocabulary gets more involved.

### Use arrow keys to navigate prior commands (work smart, not hard) {#use-arrow-keys-to-navigate-prior-commands-work-smart-not-hard}

The shell remembers commands you have already run. You do not need to retype a
long pipeline every time you want to tweak it.

- **Up arrow** — step back through previous commands
- **Down arrow** — step forward again through that history

Works in the **browser sandbox**.

This is especially useful when you are iterating on something fiddly: a **`grep`**
search (you will meet it in [section 3](#grep-chaining)), a **`curl`** HTTP call
([section 8](#probe-an-api-with-curl-and-parse-json-with-jq)), or a script you
keep running with small edits. A **pipeline** chains commands with `|` — also
coming in section 2.
Run the command once, press **Up**, adjust a word or two, press **Enter**.

### Try It

Open the sandbox and run a few different commands, then use the arrow keys to
bring an earlier one back to the prompt without retyping it.

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="shell-dock-open-btn">Open sandbox for this exercise</button>
```

### Use Tab to complete matches {#use-tab-to-complete-matches}

Tab completion is the shell's way of finishing your typing for you. Start a
command or path, press **Tab**, and the shell suggests the rest based on what
exists in your current directory or what it recognises as a valid command name.

- Type the first few letters of a filename, then press **Tab**
- If there is only one match, the shell fills in the rest
- If there are several matches, press **Tab** again (or twice quickly) to see
  the options

This saves time and cuts down on typos — particularly handy for long paths like
`project/src/eval_metrics.py` when you only need to type `project/src/e` and
hit **Tab**.

Not supported in the **browser sandbox** — practise on a **local terminal** or
in **GitHub Codespaces**.

### Try It

On your **local terminal** or in **Codespaces** (not the browser sandbox): create
a file with **`touch my-long-filename.txt`**, then type **`cat my-l`** and press
**Tab** to complete the name before pressing **Enter**.

### Jump around the command line with modifier keys {#jump-around-the-command-line-with-modifier-keys}

Once a command gets long, tapping the arrow key character-by-character is
painful. On macOS, modifier keys let you move in bigger jumps:

- **⌘ + ←** — jump to the start of the line
- **⌘ + →** — jump to the end of the line
- **⌥ + ←** — jump back one word at a time
- **⌥ + →** — jump forward one word at a time

This is useful when you need to fix a typo in the middle of a pipeline without
retyping the whole thing. Jump to the word, edit it, **Enter**.

On Linux terminals, the equivalents are usually **Ctrl+A** / **Ctrl+E** for the
start and end of the line, and **Alt + ←** / **Alt + →** to move word by word.

Not supported in the **browser sandbox** — practise on a **local terminal** or
in **GitHub Codespaces**.

### Try It

On your **local terminal** or in **Codespaces** (not the browser sandbox), type
a long command such as the one below — it uses **`grep`** (search lines),
**`wc -l`** (count lines), and **`|`** (pipe output along). You do not need to
memorise it yet; the goal is cursor practice:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
grep ERROR app.log | grep -v retry | wc -l
```

Use **⌘ + ←** and **⌥ + →** to move the cursor without retyping. On Linux, try
**Ctrl+A** and **Alt + →** instead.

### Search your command history {#search-your-command-history}

Pressing **Up** walks back one command at a time. That is fine for recent
history, but less fine when you ran something useful twenty commands ago and
only remember a fragment of it.

**Ctrl+R** starts a reverse search through your command history:

1. Press **Ctrl+R**
2. Type a few characters you remember (e.g. `grep`, `docker`, `curl`)
3. The shell shows the most recent matching command
4. Press **Ctrl+R** again to step to the next older match
5. Press **Enter** to run it, or **Esc** / the arrow keys to edit first

This pays off in specific scenarios:

- You ran a long `curl` or `docker` command yesterday and need it again
- You are debugging and want to rerun a `grep` pipeline with a small tweak
- You know *part* of a command but not enough to retype the whole thing

If **Ctrl+R** is not available, you can list and filter history manually with
the built-in **`history`** command:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
history | grep grep
```

**Ctrl+R** is not available in the **browser sandbox** — use a **local terminal**
or **GitHub Codespaces**.

### Try It

In the **sandbox**, run a few commands and use **Up** to bring an earlier one
back. For **Ctrl+R**, use your **local terminal** or **Codespaces** — reverse
search is not available in the browser sandbox.

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="shell-dock-open-btn">Open sandbox for this exercise</button>
```

### Know your `~/.zshrc` and history file {#know-your-zshrc-and-history-file}

On macOS, your default shell is usually **zsh**. When you open a new terminal
tab, zsh reads a config file in your home directory called **`~/.zshrc`**
(pronounced "zsh-R-C"). Think of it as startup instructions for your shell.

Typical things people store in `~/.zshrc`:

- **Aliases** — shortcuts for commands you use often
- **`export` lines** — environment variables such as `PATH` (where the shell
  looks for programs)
- **Tool setup** — many installers (Conda, nvm, Homebrew) ask you to paste a
  line into `~/.zshrc` so their commands work in every new terminal

That last point is often *why* you need to configure it. A tool installs
successfully, but the command is "not found" until you add its setup snippet to
`~/.zshrc` and open a fresh terminal (or run **`source ~/.zshrc`** to reload the
file into your current shell).

Your command **history** lives in a separate file — usually **`~/.zsh_history`**.
That is how **Ctrl+R** and the **Up** arrow can find commands from previous
days, not just the current session. The history file is the shell's memory;
`~/.zshrc` is its personality.

On Linux with **bash**, the same ideas apply but the files are often named
`~/.bashrc` and `~/.bash_history` instead.

The browser sandbox does not use your real `~/.zshrc` — these files matter on a
**local terminal** or in **GitHub Codespaces**.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Be careful what you put in `~/.zshrc`. It runs automatically every time you open
a terminal. Do **not** store secrets (API keys, passwords) here unless you
understand the security implications — and never commit this file to a public
repository.
:::

### Try It

On your local machine, run `echo $SHELL` to see which shell you are using, then
`ls -la ~/.zshrc ~/.zsh_history` (or `~/.bashrc` / `~/.bash_history` on Linux).
Open `~/.zshrc` in your editor and see whether you recognise any aliases or
`export` lines already there.

### Stop a runaway command with Ctrl+C {#stop-a-runaway-command-with-ctrlc}

Sometimes you paste the wrong thing, start a command that will not finish, or
realise mid-run that you made a mistake. **Ctrl+C** sends an interrupt signal
and stops the command at the current prompt.

- Press **Ctrl+C** once and wait a moment — most commands exit cleanly
- If nothing happens, press **Ctrl+C** again (some programs need a second nudge)
- You get a fresh prompt; nothing is "broken" — you can try again

This is the first reflex to build. It is faster and safer than closing the
terminal window when something is hanging.

### Try It

In the sandbox or your local terminal, run **`sleep`** (pause for N seconds) and
press **Ctrl+C** before it finishes. You should return to the prompt immediately.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
sleep 60
```

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="shell-dock-open-btn">Open sandbox for this exercise</button>
```

### When things go wrong, read the error first {#when-things-go-wrong-read-the-error-first}

Error messages look intimidating, but they usually tell you *which* of a few
common problems you hit. A quick scan saves a lot of guessing.

| Message | Likely cause | What to try |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `command not found` | Typo, or the program is not installed / not on your **`PATH`** (the list of directories the shell searches for programs) | Check spelling; run **`which`** *name* to locate a command; check install docs |
| `Permission denied` | You lack rights to read, write, or execute that file | **`ls -l`** the path (long listing shows permissions); **`chmod +x`** adds execute permission for scripts; check you own the file |
| `No such file or directory` | Wrong path, or you are in the wrong folder | **`pwd`** (print working directory); **`ls`** (list files); check for typos in the filename |

The shell is not scolding you — it is pointing at the mismatch between what you
asked for and what exists on disk (or in your `PATH`).

### Try It

In the sandbox, trigger each error on purpose and read the message before fixing
it:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
typo_command          # command not found
cat secret.txt          # no such file (until you create it)
touch locked.txt && chmod 000 locked.txt && cat locked.txt   # permission denied
```

**`touch`** creates an empty file; **`chmod`** changes permissions (`000` removes
all access, so `cat` fails). **`&&`** runs the next command only if the previous
one succeeded.

```{=html}
<button type="button" class="shell-dock-open-btn">Open sandbox for this exercise</button>
```

### Quote paths and patterns carefully {#quote-paths-and-patterns-carefully}

The shell splits your command on **spaces** unless you tell it not to. Quotes
control that — and they behave differently.

- **Single quotes `'...'`** — everything inside is literal. No variable expansion.
- **Double quotes `"..."`** — variables like `$HOME` expand; most other
  characters are literal.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
FILE="my report.txt"
touch "$FILE"           # creates one file with a space in the name
touch $FILE             # without quotes: tries to create two files (my, report.txt)

grep 'ERROR' app.log    # pattern is literal — good for fixed strings
grep "level=$LOG_LEVEL" app.log   # double quotes when you need a variable inside
```

If a path or filename might contain spaces, wrap it in **double quotes**. If you
are passing a fixed pattern to **`grep`** (search lines), **single quotes** are
often simpler.

When you expand a variable in a path, wrap it in double quotes — `"$TARGET"`
treats the whole value as one path even when it contains spaces.

### Try It

Create a file with a space in the name, then `cat` it with and without quotes to
see the difference:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
touch "notes draft.txt"
cat "notes draft.txt"
# cat notes draft.txt    # uncomment to see the error
```

### Environment variables and `.env` files {#environment-variables}

An **environment variable** is a named value the shell (and child programs) can
read. You set one for the current session like this:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
export MODEL_NAME=gpt-4o-mini
echo $MODEL_NAME
```

- **`export`** makes the variable visible to commands you run from this shell
- **`echo $NAME`** prints the current value (the `$` tells the shell to expand it)
- Variables set this way last until you close the terminal tab

Putting `export` lines in `~/.zshrc` (see above) makes them available every
time you open a new terminal. That is fine for non-secret defaults like
`export EDITOR=code`.

For **API keys and tokens**, prefer a **`.env` file** in your project root
instead of hard-coding secrets in your shell config:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
# .env — loaded by your app or tooling, not committed to git
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
LOG_LEVEL=info
```

Most Python and Node AI stacks load `.env` automatically (via `python-dotenv`,
`dotenv`, or framework conventions). Add `.env` to `.gitignore` so secrets never
land in a public repository.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Never paste API keys into the browser sandbox, commit them to git, or store
them in a public gist. Use `.env` locally and platform secret stores in CI
(GitHub Actions secrets, etc.).
:::

For a one-off command in your terminal, you can set a variable inline without
touching a file. **`curl`** fetches a URL over HTTP ([section 8](#probe-an-api-with-curl-and-parse-json-with-jq));
**`head`** prints the first few lines of output — handy when a response is long:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-your-key curl -s https://api.openai.com/v1/models | head
```

That sets the variable only for that single command — useful for quick tests,
but `.env` is easier to maintain across a project.

### Try It

In the sandbox, set a variable and read it back:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
export DEMO_VAR=hello-shell
echo $DEMO_VAR
echo "Model would be: $DEMO_VAR"
```

## 1) Shell Fundamentals {#shell-fundamentals}

We'll begin with a tiny command set that you will use repeatedly.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
pwd          # print working directory — where am I?
ls           # list files and folders here
ls -la       # -l long format; -a include hidden (dot) entries
cd /tmp      # change directory
cd -         # jump back to previous directory
```

**`touch`** creates an empty file (or updates a timestamp). You will use it in
several challenges.

### Try It

Run the commands above in the sandbox and answer:

1. Which directory are you in?
2. Which entries are hidden (start with `.`)?
3. What changed after `cd -`?

After `cd /tmp`, run `touch /tmp/visited.txt` so the checker can confirm you
reached `/tmp`.

## 2) Data Flow: Pipes and Redirection {#data-flow-pipes-and-redirection}

The shell gets powerful when you connect simple tools together.

- **`printf`** — print formatted text (like `echo`, but handles newlines reliably)
- **`cat`** — print a file's contents to the terminal
- **`grep`** — print lines that match a pattern (more in [section 3](#grep-chaining))

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
printf "apple\nbanana\napricot\n" > fruits.txt
cat fruits.txt
grep '^a' fruits.txt
grep '^a' fruits.txt | wc -l
```

- `>` writes output to a file (overwrites existing content).
- `|` passes output from one command into the next.
- **`wc -l`** — **w**ord **c**ount, lines only. Counts how many lines are in the
  input (a file or piped output). Useful when you want a total, not every matching
  line.

### Try It

Add one more fruit with **`echo`** (quick one-line print), appending with **`>>`**
instead of overwriting with `>`:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
echo "blueberry" >> fruits.txt
grep '^b' fruits.txt | wc -l
```

## 3) Grep Chaining {#grep-chaining}

**`grep`** searches text for lines matching a pattern. It is one of the best
shell tools for quick investigations.

- **`grep 'PATTERN' file`** — lines containing `PATTERN`
- **`grep -v 'PATTERN'`** — **v**invert: lines that do *not* match (exclude noise)

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
printf "INFO startup\nWARN cache_miss\nERROR timeout\nERROR retry_failed\n" > app.log
cat app.log | grep 'ERROR' | grep -v 'retry'
```

The `^` in patterns like `'^a'` means "starts with" (used in section 2).

This approach is useful for narrowing noisy logs quickly:

1. broad match (`ERROR`)
2. exclude known noise (`-v retry`)

### AI Engineer Use Case

When a local model service fails, this pattern helps isolate relevant errors
before you disappear into a debugging rabbit hole.

### Try It

Build `app.log`, then write a pipeline that shows `ERROR` lines but excludes
anything containing `retry` or `healthcheck`:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
printf "INFO startup\nWARN cache_miss\nERROR timeout\nERROR retry_failed\nERROR healthcheck ping\n" > app.log
grep 'ERROR' app.log | grep -v retry | grep -v healthcheck
```

You should see only `ERROR timeout`. Add another line and adjust the filters
until the output matches what you expect.

## 4) Globs and Brace Expansion {#globs-and-brace-expansion}

### Globs

A **glob** is a wildcard pattern the shell uses to match filenames. Before a
command runs, the shell expands the pattern into a list of matching files.

Common wildcards:

- `*` — matches any characters (e.g. `*.json` → all `.json` files)
- `?` — matches exactly one character (e.g. `file?.txt` → `file1.txt`, `fileA.txt`)

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
ls *.txt
ls project/src/*.py
```

If you used `echo rm ./logs/*.json` earlier in the hints section, that `*` is a
glob — `echo` lets you preview which files would be matched before you run
**`rm`** (remove) for real.

### Brace expansion

Brace expansion is a different trick — it generates text from a pattern in
curly braces. It saves surprising amounts of time when scaffolding projects.

- **`mkdir`** — create a directory; **`-p`** creates parent folders too if missing
- **`ls -R`** — list recursively (every subdirectory)

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
mkdir -p project/{data,src,tests,logs}
touch project/src/{ingest,embed,serve}.py
ls -R project
```

This is great for scaffolding small prototypes quickly.

### Try It

Create a second set of files for evaluation scripts in one command.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
touch project/src/{eval_metrics,eval_runner}.py
```

## 5) Simple For Loops {#simple-for-loops}

A **for loop** runs the same commands once per item in a list. That is how you
batch-process files, hit several endpoints, or rerun a check across a folder
without copy-pasting.

Basic shape:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
for name in item1 item2 item3; do
  echo "Processing $name"
done
```

- **`for ... in ...`** — the list can be words you type, or a glob the shell expands
- **`do` / `done`** — wrap the commands to repeat
- **`$name`** — the current item (quote it as `"$name"` when it might contain spaces)

Loop over files with a glob (see [section 4](#globs-and-brace-expansion)). Here we
use **`wc -l`** on each file directly — it prints how many lines that file
contains (you met `wc -l` on piped output in section 2):

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
for f in *.txt; do
  echo "=== $f ==="
  wc -l "$f"
done
```

Quoting `"$f"` matters when filenames contain spaces — the same rule from the
[quoting hints](#quote-paths-and-patterns-carefully).

### AI Engineer Use Case

Got twelve eval output files and need the same `grep` on each? A loop beats
running the command twelve times by hand:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
for f in outputs/run_*.log; do
  echo "== $f =="
  grep 'ERROR' "$f"
done
```

### Try It

Create a small `logs/` folder with three files (**`mkdir -p`** creates the folder;
**`printf`** writes each log), then loop over every `.log` and print any line
containing `ERROR`. The **`||`** means "if the left command fails, run the right
one instead" — here, print `(no errors)` when `grep` finds nothing:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
mkdir -p logs
printf "INFO ok\n" > logs/alpha.log
printf "ERROR timeout\n" > logs/beta.log
printf "ERROR retry\nWARN slow\n" > logs/gamma.log

for f in logs/*.log; do
  echo "== $f =="
  grep 'ERROR' "$f" || echo "(no errors)"
done
```

You should see errors from `beta.log` and `gamma.log`, and `(no errors)` for
`alpha.log`. Try adding a fourth log file and rerunning the loop.

## 6) Executables and Permissions {#executables-and-permissions}

A script file is not executable by default, even if it contains valid shell
code.

- **`cat > file <<'EOF'`** — write several lines to a file (a **heredoc**); text
  until `EOF` is saved into `file`
- **`./hello.sh`** — run a script in the current directory (`./` means "here")
- **`ls -l`** — long listing; shows permission letters including `x` for executable
- **`chmod +x`** — add e**x**ecute permission so you can run the script

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
cat > hello.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Hello from shell"
EOF

ls -l hello.sh
./hello.sh
```

The first line `#!/usr/bin/env bash` is a **shebang** — it tells the system which
interpreter to use when you run `./hello.sh`.

You should see a permission error before adding execute permission. That's
normal.

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
chmod +x hello.sh
ls -l hello.sh
./hello.sh
```

This pattern matters when packaging helper scripts for teammates, automation,
or CI jobs.

### Try It

Walk through the full flow in the sandbox:

1. Create `hello.sh` with the heredoc above and run `./hello.sh` — expect a
   permission error.
2. Run `ls -l hello.sh` and note the permission string (no `x` yet).
3. Run `chmod +x hello.sh`, check `ls -l` again, then `./hello.sh` — it should
   print `Hello from shell`.

### Use a DRY_RUN flag before you trust a script {#dry-run-flag}

Once you are writing scripts, you will often touch real files, call live APIs,
or change application state — and hoping for the best is not a strategy.

A common pattern is a **DRY_RUN** flag. Instead of performing the action, the
script prints what it *would* do. You inspect the output (on screen or in a log
file). If it looks right, run again without the flag and trust the result.

Some familiar commands have a built-in safety switch. For example, **`rm`**
(remove/delete) with the **`-i`** flag asks you to confirm before each delete:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
rm -i notes.txt
```

For your own scripts, an environment variable keeps things simple:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
# safe preview
DRY_RUN=1 ./cleanup_old_embeddings.sh

# real run, only after the preview looked correct
./cleanup_old_embeddings.sh
```

A minimal pattern inside a script might look like this. **`find`** searches the
filesystem; **`-type f`** limits to files, **`-mtime +30`** finds files older than
30 days, and **`-delete`** removes them (we only run that branch when `DRY_RUN`
is not set):

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
if [ "$DRY_RUN" = "1" ]; then
  echo "Would delete files older than 30 days in ./cache/"
else
  find ./cache/ -type f -mtime +30 -delete
fi
```

You can redirect dry-run output to a log for a paper trail. **`>>`** appends
output to a file (you will not see it on screen unless you open the log):

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
DRY_RUN=1 ./cleanup_old_embeddings.sh >> dry-run.log
```

**`tee`** does both — it prints to the terminal *and* writes to the file at the
same time. That is handy when you want to inspect the preview immediately while
still keeping a record:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
DRY_RUN=1 ./cleanup_old_embeddings.sh | tee dry-run.log
```

Use `>>` when you only need the log. Use `tee` when you want to read the output
and save it in one step.

This is especially wise when a command is destructive, expensive, or hard to
undo — bulk deletes, deployment scripts, or anything that hits production data.

For quick **one-liners**, you do not always need a full script. **`echo`**
prints text to the terminal — use it to preview a destructive command first,
then run the real thing once you are satisfied:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
# preview
echo rm ./logs/*.json

# enact
rm ./logs/*.json
```

With variables or wildcard patterns like `*.json`, `echo` shows you how the
shell will expand things before anything irreversible happens:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
TARGET="./cache/embeddings"
echo rm -rf "$TARGET"
# rm -rf "$TARGET"
```

The same idea works inside pipelines. Swap the destructive command for `echo`
temporarily:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
find ./tmp -name "*.bak" -exec echo rm {} \;
# find ./tmp -name "*.bak" -exec rm {} \;
```

If the echoed output looks right, rerun without `echo` and let the command do
its job.

### Try It

In the sandbox, save the script pattern above as `dry_demo.sh` using a heredoc
(as above), make it executable with `chmod +x`, then run `DRY_RUN=1 ./dry_demo.sh`
followed by `./dry_demo.sh` and compare the behaviour. Then try
`echo rm ./welcome.txt` before actually removing anything.

## 7) Processes, Ports, and Signals {#processes-ports-and-signals}

Now we're in classic operations/debugging territory.

### Start and inspect a process

- **`sleep N`** — pause for N seconds (useful for testing)
- **`&` at the end** — run the command in the **background** so you get your prompt back
- **`jobs`** — list background tasks started from this shell
- **`ps`** — list running processes; **`-ef`** shows all processes in full format
- **PID** — **p**rocess **id**entifier; a numeric handle you pass to `kill`

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
sleep 300 &
jobs
ps -ef | grep sleep | grep -v grep
```

The second `grep -v grep` drops the `grep` process itself from the results — a
common trick when searching for processes.

### Stop a process gracefully

**`kill PID`** sends a polite shutdown signal (replace `PID` with the number from
`ps`):

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
kill <PID>
```

### Force stop (last resort)

**`kill -9 PID`** forces immediate termination — no cleanup:

::: {.callout-warning}
Use `kill -9` sparingly. It bypasses graceful shutdown and can leave temporary
state or partial writes behind.
:::

### Check which process is using a port

**`lsof`** — **l**ist **o**pen **f**iles; sockets count as files. **`-i :8000`**
shows what is bound to port 8000:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
lsof -i :8000
```

In real projects, this is often the fastest answer to:
"Why won't my service start on this port?"

Use a **local terminal** or **GitHub Codespaces** for full-fidelity process and
network debugging — the browser sandbox may not reproduce host networking behaviour.

### Try It

**In the sandbox** — start a background job and find its process ID:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
sleep 120 &
jobs
ps -ef | grep sleep | grep -v grep
```

Copy the PID from the `ps` output (the number in the second column).

**Locally or in Codespaces** — stop it gracefully, then check it is gone:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
kill <PID>
ps -ef | grep sleep | grep -v grep
```

Replace `<PID>` with the number you copied. The second `ps` should return nothing.
If `kill` or `ps` behave differently in the sandbox, run this full exercise on
your machine.

### Probe an API with `curl` (and parse JSON with `jq`) {#probe-an-api-with-curl-and-parse-json-with-jq}

AI work involves a lot of HTTP — model APIs, embedding services, health checks.
**`curl`** is the shell's Swiss Army knife for sending requests and inspecting
responses without opening Postman.

A minimal GET with the response body on stdout:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
curl -s https://httpbin.org/get
```

- **`-s`** — silent mode (hides the progress meter so pipes stay clean)

When the response is JSON, **`jq`** filters and formats it — pass a path like
`.headers.Host` to pull one field. Install `jq` locally if you do not have it
(`brew install jq` on macOS).

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
curl -s https://httpbin.org/get | jq '.headers.Host'
```

For authenticated APIs, pass the key from an environment variable (set in your
shell or loaded from `.env` — never hard-code it in the command history).
**`-H`** adds an HTTP header:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  https://api.openai.com/v1/models | jq '.data[].id'
```

You can practise the `jq` part in the sandbox without network access — save a
fake response and parse it locally:

```{.bash filename="terminal"}
printf '{"choices":[{"message":{"content":"pong"}}]}\n' > response.json
cat response.json | jq '.choices[0].message.content'
```

The browser sandbox may not include `curl`, `jq`, or outbound network access.
Run API probes on a **local terminal** or in **GitHub Codespaces**.

## 10) Pre-Publish Checklist For Your Own Shell Docs

- Are all interactive commands safe and reversible?
- Did you clearly warn readers not to paste secrets?
- Did you distinguish sandbox behavior from real host behavior?
- Are advanced commands (`kill -9`, `lsof -i`) explained with caution?
- Does each section include a concrete "why this matters" use case?

## Glossary {#glossary}

Quick reference for commands and terms in this tutorial. Each entry links to where
it is introduced — use this when you meet something unfamiliar mid-challenge.

### Concepts

- **[Background job](#processes-ports-and-signals)** — A command running while you
  keep your prompt (`sleep 300 &`).
- **[Brace expansion](#globs-and-brace-expansion)** — Generate text from a pattern
  in curly braces (`project/{data,src}`).
- **[Command](#core-vocabulary)** — A program name you type at the prompt (`ls`,
  `grep`).
- **[DRY_RUN](#dry-run-flag)** — Preview pattern: run with a flag set so nothing
  destructive happens until you are sure.
- **[Environment variable](#environment-variables)** — A named value programs can
  read (`export MODEL_NAME=...`).
- **[Flag](#core-vocabulary)** — An option after a command, usually starting with
  `-` (`ls -la`, `grep -v`).
- **[For loop](#simple-for-loops)** — Repeat commands for each item in a list
  (`for f in *.log; do ... done`).
- **[GitHub Codespaces](#choose-your-environment)** — Cloud Linux dev environment with VS
  Code and a real terminal in the browser.
- **[Glob](#globs-and-brace-expansion)** — Wildcard filename pattern (`*.json`,
  `logs/*.log`).
- **[Heredoc](#executables-and-permissions)** — Multi-line input into a file
  (`cat > file <<'EOF'`).
- **[PATH](#when-things-go-wrong-read-the-error-first)** — Directories the shell
  searches when you type a command name.
- **[PID](#processes-ports-and-signals)** — Process identifier — numeric handle for
  `kill`.
- **[Pipeline](#data-flow-pipes-and-redirection)** — Commands chained with `|`;
  output of one feeds the next.
- **[Prompt](#core-vocabulary)** — Where you type commands, usually ending in `$`.
- **[Shebang](#executables-and-permissions)** — First line of a script (`#!/usr/bin/env bash`)
  telling the system which interpreter to use.

### Commands

- **[`cat`](#data-flow-pipes-and-redirection)** — Print a file's contents.
- **[`cd`](#shell-fundamentals)** — Change directory; **`cd -`** returns to the
  previous one.
- **[`chmod`](#executables-and-permissions)** — Change permissions; **`chmod +x`**
  makes a script executable.
- **[`curl`](#probe-an-api-with-curl-and-parse-json-with-jq)** — Send HTTP
  requests from the terminal.
- **[`echo`](#data-flow-pipes-and-redirection)** — Print text (also used to preview
  destructive commands in [DRY_RUN](#dry-run-flag)).
- **[`export`](#environment-variables)** — Set an environment variable for child
  programs.
- **[`find`](#dry-run-flag)** — Search the filesystem by name, type, age, etc.
- **[`grep`](#grep-chaining)** — Search lines matching a pattern; **`-v`** inverts
  (exclude matches).
- **[`head`](#environment-variables)** — Print the first few lines of output.
- **[`history`](#search-your-command-history)** — List commands you have run in this
  session.
- **[`jobs`](#processes-ports-and-signals)** — List background tasks from this shell.
- **[`jq`](#probe-an-api-with-curl-and-parse-json-with-jq)** — Filter and format
  JSON (`jq '.field'`).
- **[`kill`](#processes-ports-and-signals)** — Send a signal to a process; **`-9`**
  forces immediate stop.
- **[`ls`](#shell-fundamentals)** — List files; **`-l`** long format; **`-a`**
  includes hidden entries; **`-R`** recursive.
- **[`lsof`](#processes-ports-and-signals)** — List open files; **`-i :PORT`** shows
  what is using a port.
- **[`mkdir`](#globs-and-brace-expansion)** — Create a directory; **`-p`** creates
  parent folders too.
- **[`printf`](#data-flow-pipes-and-redirection)** — Print formatted text (reliable
  newlines for building files).
- **[`ps`](#processes-ports-and-signals)** — List processes; **`-ef`** shows all in
  full format.
- **[`pwd`](#shell-fundamentals)** — Print working directory (where am I?).
- **[`rm`](#dry-run-flag)** — Remove files; **`-i`** asks before each delete.
- **[`sleep`](#processes-ports-and-signals)** — Pause for N seconds.
- **[`source`](#know-your-zshrc-and-history-file)** — Reload a config file into the
  current shell (`source ~/.zshrc`).
- **[`tee`](#dry-run-flag)** — Write to a file and print to the terminal at the same
  time.
- **[`touch`](#shell-fundamentals)** — Create an empty file (or update timestamp).
- **[`wc`](#data-flow-pipes-and-redirection)** — Word count; **`-l`** counts lines.
- **[`which`](#when-things-go-wrong-read-the-error-first)** — Show path to a command
  executable.

### Operators and syntax

- **[`&`](#processes-ports-and-signals)** — Run a command in the background.
- **[`&&`](#when-things-go-wrong-read-the-error-first)** — Run the next command only
  if the previous one succeeded.
- **[`||`](#simple-for-loops)** — Run the next command only if the previous one
  failed.
- **[`|` (pipe)](#data-flow-pipes-and-redirection)** — Send one command's output into
  the next.
- **[`>` / `>>`](#data-flow-pipes-and-redirection)** — Redirect output to a file
  (overwrite / append).
- **[`./script.sh`](#executables-and-permissions)** — Run an executable in the current
  directory.
- **[`$VAR`](#environment-variables)** — Expand an environment variable.
- **[`'...'` / `"..."`](#quote-paths-and-patterns-carefully)** — Single quotes: literal
  text. Double quotes: allow variable expansion.

### Keyboard shortcuts

- **[Ctrl+C](#stop-a-runaway-command-with-ctrlc)** — Stop a running command.
- **[Ctrl+R](#search-your-command-history)** — Reverse-search command history (not
  available in the browser sandbox).
- **[Tab](#use-tab-to-complete-matches)** — Complete filenames and command names
  (not available in the browser sandbox).
- **[Modifier keys](#jump-around-the-command-line-with-modifier-keys)** — Jump by
  word or to the start/end of the line (not available in the browser sandbox).
- **[Up / Down arrows](#use-arrow-keys-to-navigate-prior-commands-work-smart-not-hard)** —
  Step through previous commands (works in the browser sandbox).

## Further reading

A short list of resources worth your time. Each one is widely respected, free, and
does something this tutorial does not — deeper courses, correct bash habits, dense
references, or tools you will use for years.

- [**The Unix Shell** (Software Carpentry)](https://swcarpentry.github.io/shell-novice/) —
  The best structured follow-on from here. Clear lessons, exercises, and a gentle
  ramp from navigation through scripting. If you liked the hands-on style of this
  article, start here next.

- [**Bash Guide**](https://mywiki.wooledge.org/BashGuide) and [**Bash Pitfalls**](https://mywiki.wooledge.org/BashPitfalls) (Greg's Wiki) —
  The bash community's gold standard for doing things *correctly*. The guide teaches
  good habits; the pitfalls page is a catalogue of ways bash will surprise you.
  Essential once you start writing scripts that other people (or CI) will run.

- [**The Art of Command Line**](https://github.com/jlevy/the-art-of-command-line) —
  One dense page of practical CLI wisdom — file processing, debugging, one-liners,
  macOS and Windows notes. Legendary for a reason (160k+ GitHub stars). Keep it
  bookmarked and skim a section when you have five minutes.

- [**explainshell.com**](https://explainshell.com/) —
  Paste any command; get a visual breakdown of every flag and argument against the
  man page text. Invaluable when you copy a `curl`, `find`, or `tar` one-liner from
  Stack Overflow and want to know what it actually does before you run it.

- [**tldr pages**](https://tldr.sh/) —
  Practical examples for everyday commands (`tldr tar`, `tldr curl`). The man page
  when you need the full spec; tldr when you need to remember the flags you always
  forget. Install once (`brew install tldr` on macOS) and never leave home without
  it.

- [**ShellCheck**](https://www.shellcheck.net/) —
  Static analysis for shell scripts. Paste a script or hook it into your editor; it
  catches quoting bugs, portability issues, and logic traps before they bite you in
  production. Non-negotiable once you are writing glue scripts for real.

- [**Bite size bash**](https://wizardzines.com/zines/bite-size-bash/) (Julia Evans) —
  A short, illustrated zine on how bash *actually* works — quoting, `if` tests,
  variables, and the gotchas experienced programmers still trip over. Her
  [terminal deep-dives](https://jvns.ca/blog/2025/06/24/new-zine--the-secret-rules-of-the-terminal/)
  are excellent if you want to understand *why* the terminal feels inconsistent
  (spoiler: it is four different programs pretending to be one).

## Wrap-up

Shell skills compound quickly. Start with navigation and pipes, add pattern
matching and loops, then permissions and process control, and apply them to your
own tool chain. Once these habits click, the shell becomes a dependable
orchestration layer for AI engineering work. Keep the [Glossary](#glossary) handy
when you forget a flag or command name.
